items.question: What appealed to you about Douglas Hofstadter’s Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid when you first read it after college?
items.object: Douglas Hofstadter's book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
items.answer: Well, right after I graduated from college, I read Douglas Hofstadter's book Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid, which probably a lot of the listeners here have read or maybe at least own. I don't know how much they've read; it's a long book, but I was incredibly inspired by the ideas in that book. I came out of college as a mathematics major, so I was really excited about the mathematics part of it. I also was really into music, especially Baroque and classical music, so the part about Bach was really exciting to me, and in particular, the ideas about AI, which I knew absolutely nothing about at the time.

items.question: How do you see the intellectual focus of your work in Douglas Hofstadter’s group as differing from other AI research at the time?
items.object: The research approach in Douglas Hofstadter’s group
items.answer: Hofstadter also didn't have a computer science background. He has a PhD in physics and never really saw himself as a computer scientist. In fact, at Michigan he was in the psychology department, interestingly, and while I was in computer science, our offices were all in psychology, so we spent our time hanging out with the psychology faculty and grad students. I think at least my interest, and the interest of other people in our group, was more on the side of how do we understand intelligence more broadly than individual human intelligence, or how do we understand the nature of understanding, of being able to make analogies. That was really the focus, rather than any desire to build AI systems for a particular application. So it was much more basic research, much more inspired by what's now called cognitive science, and I think that made the research very different from what a lot of other people in AI were doing.

items.question: How do you see today's debates about symbolic AI and learning in relation to the debates you encountered when you were starting out in AI?
items.object: Recurring debates in AI about symbolic methods, connectionism, and innateness versus learning
items.answer: Those debates are very similar to the kinds of debates we're having today. The question of symbolic AI versus machine learning, or subsymbolic AI, was at the forefront back then as it is today. I got my PhD in 1990, so there was a lot of work on people doing symbolic stuff versus what was called PDP, parallel distributed processing, and connectionism. All of that was very big. There were also debates like the ones we're having today on innateness versus learning: how much should be built into a system versus how much should be learned end to end. These debates never change. The people having them change, but the debates stay the same.

items.question: How do you think the success of statistical machine learning has changed the debates within AI?
items.object: The evolution of AI debates in light of statistical machine learning’s success
items.answer: In some cases we're saying the same things. In some cases I think they've evolved. Back then, questions about statistical machine learning were just kind of getting started, and a lot of people never thought that it would achieve the kinds of things that it has achieved. No one thought that speech recognition would be essentially solved, at least to some extent, by statistical learning. Nobody thought that language processing would get as far as it did without building in structures of grammar and syntax and all of that. A lot of people were quite surprised at how powerful this massive data-driven statistical learning has become. I've definitely been surprised, but I also think that that impressive success has influenced a lot of people to extrapolate how far scaling can actually go, just in terms of data and model size. I think that debate is new: whether scaling will take us to the next big step in AI progress or whether it's going to hit a dead end at some point.

items.question: How do you judge whether current language-model metrics and benchmarks capture real progress in AI?
items.object: Language-model evaluation metrics and benchmarks
items.answer: I'm not sure we have the right metrics for this empirical study. When we look at language models, how do we evaluate them? How do we say that we're making progress? One way is that we look at measures like perplexity, information-theoretic kinds of measures about the distribution that's being learned. We also look at benchmark datasets, and one of the things we've seen is that some of these benchmark datasets are flawed in terms of allowing statistical shortcuts that enable a system to do well on these benchmarks without having the real ability the benchmark is trying to measure. You see this with things like the General Language Understanding Evaluation, the GLUE and SuperGLUE language benchmarks. They have a lot of problems that humans, or subtle things humans, would never pick up on because humans are using their understanding of language to answer the questions, but these systems that have enormous capacity for learning correlations can pick up on. When we talk about progress in natural language understanding or other areas of AI, we don't quite have the right benchmarks to assess that, and that's one reason these systems are really impressive when you interact with them, but they haven't yet made the jump in many cases to being used in the real world because they're too brittle.

items.question: How do you see the comparison between current AI systems and thought experiments like the Chinese room or philosophical zombies?
items.object: The Chinese room argument and philosophical zombies as comparisons for current AI systems
items.answer: I think there's a little bit of difference with the Chinese room and zombies and all of that, where the underlying assumption there is that they actually do have human-like performance, that they aren't brittle, right? Yet they're using some kind of nonhuman-like mechanisms, whereas we haven't gotten to that point yet with AI systems. Of course, you're right that there is that problem, that it's hard to look under the hood and say how exactly is this doing the task?

items.question: Why do you question the idea that successes on narrow AI tasks represent progress toward general AI?
items.object: The first-step fallacy in interpreting progress toward general AI
items.answer: One of the fallacies I saw was what's called the first-step fallacy. This was, I think, first described by the philosopher Hubert Dreyfus back in the 1980s. This was the fallacy that any time we make progress on some narrow task, that counts as progress on general AI. Think about Deep Blue beating Kasparov at chess or AlphaGo beating the best Go players. A lot of people interpreted those huge steps as progress in general AI, but of course the techniques of Deep Blue, the sort of brute-force search, did not extend to other domains. It remains to be seen if something like deep reinforcement learning, the AlphaGo variety, can extend to anything besides games. Some of those techniques have been useful in other domains, but it's not clear that this is the continuous path we're on towards general AI. Dreyfus himself said there's a discontinuity, which he said was common sense.

items.question: Why do you regard human judgments of task difficulty as misleading guides to what AI should find easy?
items.object: The assumption that human task difficulty predicts AI task difficulty
items.answer: What I called “easy things are easy and hard things are hard” is the fallacy that if something's easy for humans it should be easy for AI, and vice versa. Something like playing Go at the highest level is very hard for humans, but it's not the hardest thing for AI systems. I like the example Gary Marcus had in one of his papers, that playing charades, which any six-year-old can do, is way beyond any current AI right now because it involves so much social knowledge and theory of mind and language and all of that. That's an easy thing for us, but still much harder for AI than Go. The easy things, things that we look at in children as the easiest things, like just having general common sense, turn out to be a grand challenge for AI. DARPA, the DoD research funding agency, has set up as a grand challenge getting an AI system with the common sense of an 18-month-old baby. We often think that the things we do so easily are also going to be easier for AI, so that's a source of over-optimism.

items.question: What do you find misleading about describing AI systems such as IBM Watson as reading or understanding?
items.object: Wishful mnemonics and anthropomorphic descriptions of AI
items.answer: What I call the lure of wishful mnemonics is a term due to Drew McDermott. A wishful mnemonic is using a term that's sort of anthropomorphic to describe an AI system. If we say that, for instance, IBM's Watson program understands natural language—one of the things they said is it can read all of the medical texts in the world in seconds—“read” implies something when we're using it in the human sense. When I say, “Oh, I read such-and-such a book,” you assume that I understood what I read. That's not what Watson is doing, at least not in the same way we are. So it's using these terms to describe what machines have done when actually they aren't doing that thing; they're doing something quite different.

items.question: How do you understand the problem with assuming that mimicking the brain is enough to capture intelligence?
items.object: The assumption that intelligence is entirely in the brain
items.answer: The fourth fallacy I identified was “intelligence is all in the brain.” That's the embodiment issue: whether mimicking our brains is enough to capture intelligence. A lot of people in cognitive science would argue that our bodies and our physical interactions with the environment, our social interactions, and all of that are absolutely essential for capturing intelligence, and this is not something AI is focusing a lot on.

items.question: How do you think the apparent ease of everyday human perception shaped expectations about recreating it in AI?
items.object: The apparent ease of human common-sense perception and early AI optimism
items.answer: We all know that machines are much better at arithmetic than humans, and they have all kinds of different abilities. But if you're trying to capture human-like intelligence, which is generally what people are doing in AI, especially if you're using your own subjective experience of having intelligence, there are certain things that just seem immediate to you, that don't seem hard at all. We're having this conversation, or I'm looking at you and I can tell that it's daytime because I see sunlight, and you're wearing a sweater so it must be kind of cold inside. I can tell you're at home, and all kinds of things. These things are immediate to us, and there was a sort of assumption: how hard could it be to capture these things? This was sort of at the beginning of the AI enterprise, even back at the original Dartmouth conference that really kicked off the field. There was this idea that they'd be able to capture all of this kind of common-sense, human-like, immediate perception very quickly.

items.question: How do you think about whether AI should replicate human-like intelligence?
items.object: Human-like and non-human-like intelligence as goals for AI
items.answer: AI people have a lot of different goals in mind, and it's not like a unified thing where everybody has the same goals. I think the original goals of the field were really to capture human-like intelligence, but there's obviously a lot of benefit in non-human-like intelligence. We see that with some of these efforts to apply AI to scientific discovery. For instance, the AlphaFold program was able, because it's so different from the way humans work, to find really interesting patterns useful for prediction in protein sequences. That's a clear intelligence-augmentation result. On the other hand, if we want AI systems to work in the human social world, the human physical world, where they're interacting with humans, like a self-driving car, we don't want them to think very differently from us. That would result in disaster, as it has in some cases, if they perceive the world in a different way than we perceive it, because that world is a world of human concepts. I think it really depends on what you want your AI system to do.

items.question: How useful do you find the term “intelligence” for thinking about AI?
items.object: The term intelligence and its influence on AI
items.answer: I think maybe the word itself is too broad to be very useful. We talk about it in so many different ways: intelligence as being on a scale, like an IQ scale, or different kinds of intelligences, like humans versus octopuses, which is a very different niche, succeeding in its niche through its kind of intelligence. We talk about AI systems as having intelligence. My GPS navigator on my phone is quite intelligent; it can figure out which route I should take because it has a lot of information and a lot of ability for optimization that I don't have. I don't know. Intelligence might just be the thing that's holding us back, that terminology. In the history of AI, at the Dartmouth meeting there was a lot of argument about what the field should be called. John McCarthy, who coined the term artificial intelligence, was trying to figure out a way to distinguish AI from neural networks, which was another field called self-organizing networks. He wanted these to be two different things, so that's why we're calling it AI, and now it's all been brought together again. Herbert Simon wanted to call it complex information processing, to get away from this idea that we're trying to mimic human intelligence. Words matter, and it may be that that word has pushed the field in certain ways that it's hard to get out of. Intelligence is hard to define because it has so many different meanings, and we really have to use adjectives now to talk about it.

items.question: How useful do you find defining intelligence as the capacity to achieve goals when discussing living things and AI systems?
items.object: Goal-based definitions of intelligence in living things and AI systems
items.answer: I don't think it's totally true that everything has some degree of intelligence. If we define it extremely broadly as being able to have goals and achieve them, every living thing has intelligence to some degree, because evolution gives the goal of surviving and procreating, and every evolved system has some way of achieving its goals. But of course that's such a broad definition it's not super useful for saying whether a GPT-3 has intelligence or a goal or anything like that. This gets into a big philosophical discussion. A lot of people in AI talk about intelligence as the capacity to achieve one's goals, but how do those goals come from? How do these goals get into these systems? I think there's a big difference between me having a goal, whatever goals I have as a living system, and something like AlphaGo having a goal. I think those are two different uses of the word, and we conflate them, which makes it hard to talk about what intelligence is in these systems.

items.question: What do you find problematic about predictions that AI will achieve human-level intelligence by 2040?
items.object: Predictions of human-level intelligence in AI
items.answer: When I see people make predictions like, “Oh, we're going to have human-level intelligence by 2040 in AI,” I think it's a problem because the target isn't well defined. What is this human-level intelligence you're calling? What are the criteria for it? If you talk about being able to do any cognitive task that a human can do, what does that even include? I don't think we have a clear sense of the target. A lot of people have the faith that we'll know it when we see it, but I'm not so convinced, because a lot of the things that underlie our intelligence, that are subconscious and that we're barely even aware of, are a huge part of it. We don't necessarily think of them as key to intelligence. A lot of people think we can sift it off our brains and put it in computers without looking carefully at all the social, physical, cultural, and other processes it's grounded in.

items.question: How do you interpret the limitations of text-to-image systems in understanding the images they create?
items.object: The semantic abilities and limitations of text-to-image systems
items.answer: I think it's again surprising how much statistical learning can accomplish given enough data, but you can still see aspects of brittleness in these systems that show they haven't really grasped the semantics of the images they're creating. There's been a lot of probing of these systems and looking at problems they have with physical reasoning. If you ask a system to order blocks—put a yellow block on top of a green block on top of a blue block—they can't do it. If you ask them to create an image that doesn't have something, like I tried a fruit bowl with no apples, they cannot do it, just because those kinds of basic concepts are not something it can get from its training data and its correlations. These failure modes are interesting because they show what these statistical algorithms are able to capture and what they aren't. It remains to be seen how much scaling will help, but I think there's something about our human experience of interacting with the physical world that these systems don't have, and therefore they're never going to get to the kind of semantic abilities that people have. That's not necessarily a generally held view, but I believe that.

items.question: How do you assess whether generative models that associate text with images are learning causal models of the world?
items.object: Generative models’ ability to learn causality
items.answer: There have been arguments over whether these generative models are able to learn causality in some way. Some people have argued that they have some notion of causality, but clearly they don't have the capacities that we have, even young children. They're associating text with configurations of pixels and embeddings of those two things. I don't think they're developing causal models of the world. Whether something like that could happen by some other learning method or other kind of data, I think is an open question.

items.question: How do you understand the role of analogy in everyday human thought and language?
items.object: Analogy in everyday human thought and language
items.answer: This goes back to my work with Douglas Hofstadter. Hofstadter's obsession is with analogies and abstraction. To him, analogy goes way beyond, say, the word analogies we're all familiar with, like “shoe is to foot as glove is to blank.” People have looked at that, but analogies are much more subtle and much richer. If someone describes a situation to you, like losing their luggage at the airport, that brings up all kinds of memories that have the kind of essence of that situation, even though they're quite different. You've sort of abstracted the essence of a particular situation, and we make analogies all the time unconsciously. Hofstadter and his colleague Emanuel Sander wrote this book called Surfaces and Essences, which is all about the various ways in which people make analogies unconsciously. It's amazing once you start to notice it how often it happens. I remember giving a talk about analogy, and there was this guy in the audience who was very skeptical. He said, “Why are you always putting analogy in the driver's seat?” It's like, okay, you just made an analogy. He didn't even notice it. Our language is full of that kind of thing.

items.question: Why do you see abstraction and transfer learning as central problems for AI?
items.object: Abstraction and transfer learning as problems for AI
items.answer: The idea is that this is something that is very easy for us but very difficult for machines. People have been working on this for decades, and we still don't have machines that can very generally make abstractions. Machine learning has this subfield called transfer learning, which is how do you take something you've learned in one domain and apply it in another domain? It's very hard, but that's just another word for analogy in my mind. I think this is one of the key problems for making AI systems that are not brittle, that can actually use knowledge they have about one kind of situation and apply it to new situations.

items.question: What do you find valuable about François Chollet's Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus as a benchmark for AI?
items.object: François Chollet's Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus
items.answer: I really like the work of François Chollet on his Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. It's a very nice benchmark for abstraction that has to do with visual transformations of little colored grids. It's a very rich domain, and nobody's been able to make much progress on it yet because we haven't captured the ability to make abstractions from a small number of examples. Few-shot learning is key; abstraction is needed for that, and I think nobody knows how to get machines to do it.

items.question: How do you distinguish having a concept from recognizing a category in AI?
items.object: Concepts as generative models rather than categories
items.answer: Often I think in AI people conflate the term concept with the term category. They say, okay, the ImageNet dataset has a thousand concepts: golden retriever, temple, coffee cup, and all that. But a concept to me is something much richer than a category. I really like another quotation from Lawrence Barsalou, a cognitive psychologist, who said a concept, having a concept, is having the ability to generate infinite instantiations of a category. An example I often use in my talk is the concept of a bridge. We think about the Golden Gate Bridge or the Brooklyn Bridge, but we can take that concept and extend it infinitely. I can talk about bridging the gender gap or the bridge of a song, if you're into music. You have these metaphorical extensions of this category, and it's the collection of all those potential instantiations of a category that make up a concept. I think of a concept not necessarily as a thing sitting statically in your brain, but more as a model that can do generation, a generative model that can generate instantiations of things.

items.question: How do you view the hypothesis that all our concepts ultimately bottom out in basic physical experience?
items.object: The hypothesis that concepts bottom out in basic physical experience
items.answer: I don't know the answer. I like the work of George Lakoff, who looks at concepts as sort of bottoming out with basic physical experience. This also relates to work by people like Elizabeth Spelke, a cognitive psychologist, who looks at what she thinks of as the innate knowledge systems that babies are born with and that we base all of our concepts on. Lakoff talks about metaphor and says the way we think about abstract things like love or money or time is all based on metaphors for physical experiences. We talk about falling in love, or time passing us by, so we think about time as a physical thing that's passing and that time goes backwards or forwards like a spatial system. He and Mark Johnson have this great book called Metaphors We Live By, which goes into great detail about all of this. I think that's a great hypothesis: that all our concepts basically bottom out in basic physical experience, basic physical knowledge of the world that maybe we're born with, maybe we learn, but are sort of primed by evolution to learn. That's a view I have sympathy with, and what it tells us is that maybe we should be looking to some of these ideas from developmental psychology to think about AI. Some people are looking more deeply at how children learn, and it's a very different way than our current machines learn, but maybe it has some insight into how to get machines to do few-shot abstraction that's robust.

items.question: How do you see the value of idealized domains such as Copycat for studying abstraction and analogy in AI?
items.object: Idealized domains such as Copycat for studying abstraction and analogy in AI
items.answer: The first thing to say is that one way to approach these questions about abstraction and analogy is to try and idealize them, not just jump at real-world behavior immediately, but say, let's take some of the issues of abstraction, like learning this richer concept and being able to use it in different situations, and make that more abstract. That's been done for a really long time. The thing I heard about first was what are called the Bongard problems, a set of visual puzzles created in the 1960s by Bongard, a Russian computer scientist who was looking at neural networks. Hofstadter wrote about this in Gödel, Escher, Bach, and one of his goals was to build a machine that could solve these problems. But then he decided this was too difficult, that he needed to idealize it even more. So he came up with this letter-string analogy domain, now called the Copycat domain, with problems that are transformations between letter strings, like ABC changes to ABD; what does PQRS change to? There's no correct answer, because you could say the last letter in the string changes to D, or it changes to ABD—anything changes to ABD, being very literal. Most people will say ABC to ABD, PQRS to PQRT. They'll take a more abstract view of what happened. Hofstadter and his students, and then when I joined the group a little bit later, me as well, created thousands and thousands of these letter-string problems. It seems like a really simple domain, but it's incredibly open-ended and richer than you might think. My PhD project was creating a computer program that could solve these problems, and it was called Copycat. It was more of a symbolic kind of system, and I think it was limited in ways that symbolic AI is limited, but it had some interesting ideas. Chollet much later was not aware of Copycat or the Bongard problems, I think, and he created his own version, the ARC Corpus, but it has a lot of the same flavor to it. These things are still challenges for AI. A good and important question is, if a program could solve these, how could it be extended to real-world analogies and abstractions? I think that's still an open question, but I do think it's a promising way to approach these issues.

items.question: How do you assess probabilistic program induction as an approach to abstraction in AI?
items.object: Probabilistic program induction as an approach to abstraction in AI
items.answer: I've been looking deeply into what's called probabilistic program induction. The idea is, if you're given some kind of abstraction problem or new situation, to represent the concept as a program. This is work done by Josh Tenenbaum and Brenden Lake and many other people. You have some set of primitives—this is your built-in knowledge—which are in the form of program primitives in some domain-specific language. Then your task as a program-induction system, given a new situation, is to create a program that will allow you to answer a question or deal with a situation. The problem with it is it's very compute-intensive; it uses a lot of expensive search. Now people are looking at speeding it up using neural networks to help speed up the search, sort of the way they were used in deep reinforcement learning with Monte Carlo search. I'm fascinated by that, but to me one problem with neural nets and this program-induction approach is it's not very dynamic. Neural networks are feed-forward; for the most part they don't have the kind of feedback we humans bring when we're trying to make sense of a situation.

items.question: Where do you see opportunities for someone starting out in AI research without huge compute resources?
items.object: Open research questions in AI and the need for large compute resources
items.answer: It's difficult to answer because AI is so broad, but there is this perception in the field that a lot of big problems have been solved, which I think is not true at all, and that you can't do anything unless you have some huge compute resource, which very few people in academia have. I think these are wrong. There are big questions people can make progress on. It really depends on your interests, but there's been so much work on deep learning with so little science behind it, so little understanding of why deep learning might work the way it does, what its limitations might be, how language models work, how they do what they do. These are all things that can be probed and studied without huge compute resources, I think, and are still big open questions. This whole question of few-shot learning, abstraction, and analogy is still wide open. I do think there are a lot of wide-open questions.
